newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says still room for discussion on tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says still room for discussion on tax reform.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, in an apparent attempt to ease tensions over the government's planned tax reform, said on Monday there was still room for discussion about the tax changes and when they should be implemented.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel raised objections to some of the proposals presented last week by Wolfgang Schaeuble, a key Kohl ally and leader of the Christian Democratic (CDU) parliamentary group.

"What we have proposed is in no way the new tax law," Kohl told reporters ahead of a meeting of CDU party leaders, adding that the proposals must be discussed within the centre-right coalition government and with the federal states.
"If it were up to me we could carry out a tax reform from one day to the next," he said. "But the books have to balance."
Kohl indicated that he was more open than in the past to introducing the tax reform in 1998, as called for by his junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP).
The FDP wants to introduce the tax cuts ahead of the next general election, which must take place by December 1998. But the CDU has until now preferred a tax reform in 1999.

The CDU last week made proposals for the tax reform that would cut taxes by a net 30 billion marks by lowering tax rates, broaden the overall tax base, eliminate loopholes and tighten rules on capital gains taxes.
The CDU plan would slash Germany's top income tax rate to 35 percent from the current 53 percent and cut the minimum rate to less than 20 percent from the current 26 percent.

CDU party leaders were meeting at the party's Bonn headquarters to discuss the proposals of the party's tax commission. The proposals will be presented at the CDU party congress at the end of October.

But Waigel, a member of the Bavarian CDU sister-party Christian Social Union, took issue with the proposals to tighten taxes on capital gains, which he said could have a negative impact on investment in Germany.

"The CDU proposal did not get my vote. The impact on Frankfurt as a place to do business has yet to be examined," Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in an interview with the weekly news magazine Focus.
The CDU plan would tax capital gains on all sales of securities or real estate, not just "speculative" sales of assets held less than six months, the current German practice.
"That is an unequal treatment of income. The point is to treat it the same," Schaeuble said when he presented the plan.
An exception would be made for primary residences.
The issue also comes just as the government is preparing the 15-billion-mark floation of a big chunk of Deutsche Telekom AG, the state-owned telephone monopoly.
Analysts fear the proposals could stifle private investor interest just as many Germans look set to buy shares for the first time, when Telekom goes public next month.
But the CDU plan would also restrict companies' leeway to set aside tax-free reserves, and limit depreciation write-offs.
The plan also calls for the elimination of current tax exemptions for income from Sunday, holiday or night work. Rules on business expenses would also be tightened.
Church tax and charitable donations would continue to be deductible.
